summary:
As a state of Mexico, Oaxaca stands under the national framework in which legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state mapping (11 and 31 March 2025) records administrative name and gender-marker changes on birth certificates in 21 of Mexico's 32 states, guided by a 2019 Supreme Court ruling that set recognition standards and was extended to adolescents and children in March 2022. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Oaxaca is among the states that have built the procedure. A 2019 reform of the state civil code created an administrative route to legal gender recognition, a 2021 decree extended it to people aged 12 and over, and a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopened access for children under 12. The resulting law is confined to identity documents; it does not determine where trans inmates are held.

The exclusionary signal a visitor may encounter is documented from the festival floor. On 25 May 2024 the organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer Goola 'Lado Sur' festival in Juchitán circulated a written invitation stating that men dressed as women would not be admitted. Muxe activists, among them defender Felina Santiago, whose advocacy spans three decades, filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body. Three velas proceeded on 26 May, with muxes affirming their place in local society and culture.

Violence forms the sharpest part of the risk picture. Trendencias reported in April 2025 that Oaxaca is Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and at the same time its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community, with violent incidents under investigation in municipalities where armed groups operate and with possible municipal-police involvement. The murdered include muxe Cristian Hernandez Cutino, aged 31, and stylist Zulma Hernandez Mendoza, aged 43. The state response described in that reporting is stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The ombudsman's own caseload shows the persistence of the pattern. Oaxaca's Defensoría del Pueblo opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022, and violence against muxes continues: muxe teacher Marimar 'Estrellita' Santiago was killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec in the Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

Formal rights and their delivery diverge across Mexico. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) finds that the country's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the analysis must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
tangentialFactors:
Inter-American and national authorities have treated impunity as the binding problem. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Violence against trans people intensified nationally over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, with the killings drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Recognition barriers elsewhere in Mexico illustrate what obstructed documentation costs. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, set against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap: Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level, with same-sex marriage legal since 2009 and Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
localsOnly:
Residents of Oaxaca can use an administrative procedure created by the 2019 civil-code reform to change name and gender marker on birth certificates, after the 2021 decree set the threshold at age 12 and the June 2023 Supreme Court ruling opened the route to children under 12.

Discriminatory exclusion can be challenged through a complaint to the national equality body, the route muxe defenders used against the Juchitán vela invitation of May 2024. Attacks on LGBTIQ+ people can be reported to the Oaxaca Defensoría del Pueblo, which opened 34 such investigations between 2015 and 2022.

Muxe community organisation is a standing feature of public life in the Istmo, with figures such as Felina Santiago carrying out decades of advocacy and muxes asserting their role in local culture through the annual velas.

Marriage equality and document-level recognition are in force; the Oaxaca gender-identity law addresses identity documents only and does not govern the placement of trans inmates in state custody.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Oaxaca provides a specific hate-crime enhancement for offences motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation, and the penalties attached, is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved here.

The characterisation of Oaxaca as Mexico's most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community rests on a single April 2025 outlet profile; the comparative ranking method behind it is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Investigations into the violent incidents reported in 2025, including any allegation of municipal-police participation, are stated as under investigation in the source; no sourced outcome is available and the matter remains unresolved.

The relationship between Oaxaca's administrative recognition procedure and the operation of the June 2023 Supreme Court ruling in practice, including processing times and refusals experienced by applicants, is not documented in this inventory and remains unresolved.

Provision for the placement of trans inmates in Oaxaca's prisons is identified only by its absence from the state's gender-identity law; no sourced policy exists in this inventory.
